notes.meaning: Israel camped at Shittim, a fertile grove of acacia trees east of the Jordan River. This was their final stop before entering Canaan. Instead of preparing for the promised land, the men fell into sexual sin with Moabite women, falling into the trap planned by Balaam.

The foreign women invited the Israelite men to their religious feasts. The men ate the meat dedicated to foreign gods and bowed down in idol worship. Giving in to physical lust led directly to spiritual unfaithfulness.

Israel attached itself to the false god called Baal of Peor, a local Canaanite deity honored on Mount Peor. By joining these immoral rites, the people broke their covenant with the true God. This open rebellion brought the Lord's burning anger against them in the form of a deadly plague.

The Lord ordered Moses to assemble the leaders and execute the guilty offenders publicly in daylight. Displaying the bodies openly demonstrated that God's justice was being carried out. This swift action was necessary to turn away God's fierce anger from the whole nation.

Moses instructed the tribal judges to carry out God's command within their own groups. Each judge was responsible for executing any men under his charge who had worshiped Baal of Peor. God's leaders were expected to uphold righteousness without showing favoritism.

While Moses and the congregation were weeping in repentance at the tabernacle gate, an Israelite man openly brought a Midianite noblewoman into the camp. This act was an astonishing display of arrogance that defied God, Moses, and the sorrow of the people.

Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron the high priest, saw this brazen sin and acted immediately. He grabbed a spear, followed the couple into their tent, and ran them both through. Because divine justice was carried out against this defiance, the deadly plague that was striking Israel stopped.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view verses 6 to 18 as coming from a separate Priestly source that was later woven together with the earlier narrative in verses 1 to 5.

notes.meaning: A total of twenty-four thousand Israelites died because of this rebellion. The high death toll showed the heavy cost of abandoning God. When the apostle Paul mentions twenty-three thousand in 1 Corinthians, commentators note he may refer only to those who died of the disease in a single day, while Moses includes all who died, including those executed by the judges.

The Lord told Moses that Phinehas had turned His anger away from Israel. Phinehas shared God's own burning concern for holiness and truth among the people. Because he stood up for God's honor, the Lord did not destroy the entire nation.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The Eastern Orthodox Church commemorates Phinehas as a righteous saint, honoring his bold zeal for preserving the holiness of Israel.

notes.meaning: God gave Phinehas a special covenant of peace. This pledge guaranteed God's friendship and blessing to him and his family. Because Phinehas worked to restore peace between God and Israel, God gave him the responsibility of keeping that peace.

This promise established a lasting priesthood for Phinehas and his family line. By judging evil, he made atonement, which means he cleared the guilt of sin and reconciled the people to God. His passionate defense of God's holiness pointed forward to the ultimate work of Christ.

differ.view: Methodists view this promise of priesthood as conditional, meaning it could be set aside if descendants sinned, as seen later with Eli's family.
Some evangelical interpreters understand this pledge as an irrevocable covenant of grace that God faithfully kept without breaking.

notes.meaning: The text identifies the defiant offenders by name to mark their perpetual dishonor. The man was Zimri, a tribal leader from Simeon, and the woman was Cozbi, daughter of a Midianite chief. Their high rank showed how deeply the rot had reached into Israel's leadership, and it highlighted Phinehas's courage in confronting powerful people.

The Lord commanded Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies and attack them. The Midianites had used deceitful traps rather than open warfare to draw Israel into immorality and idol worship at Peor. God called His people to wage holy war against the source of their spiritual corruption.
